hints: List all ions present from $\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4$ and from water, then compare ease of discharge of $\text{OH}^-$ versus $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ at the anode and $\text{H}^+$ versus $\text{Na}^+$ at the cathode.
walkthrough:
Sort out which ions can move to each electrode**
In solution you have $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ from the salt, plus $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{OH}^-$ from water. Positive ions go to the cathode, negative ions go to the anode, so it is a competition at each electrode.

Apply the water discharge rule**
Sodium is very reactive, so $\text{H}^+$ from water is discharged far more easily than $\text{Na}^+$. Sulfate is very stable, so $\text{OH}^-$ from water is discharged far more easily than $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$. That means you are effectively electrolysing water, liberating $\text{H}_2$ at the cathode and $\text{O}_2$ at the anode.

Final answer: anode: oxygen, $\text{O}_2$
cathode: hydrogen, $\text{H}_2$

hints: Convert the time to seconds and use $Q = It$ to find the total charge passed in coulombs.
Divide the charge by the Faraday constant, $96500 \text{ C mol}^{-1}$, to get moles of electrons transferred.
Use the half equations $2\text{Cl}^- \rightarrow \text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{e}^-$ and $\text{Na}^+ + \text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Na}$ to link moles of electrons to moles of $\text{Cl}_2$ and $\text{Na}$.
Convert moles of $\text{Cl}_2$ to volume using $24 \text{ dm}^3 \text{ mol}^{-1}$ at room conditions, and moles of $\text{Na}$ to mass using $23.0 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Calculate the total charge passed**
Current must be in amps and time in seconds. Think of charge as the total push of electrons:
$$Q = It$$
$$Q = 4.50 \times 1.50 \times 60 \times 60 = 24300 \text{ C}$$

Convert charge to moles of electrons**
One mole of electrons carries $96500 \text{ C}$, called the Faraday constant:
$$n(\text{e}^-) = \frac{Q}{F} = \frac{24300}{96500} = 0.252 \text{ mol}$$

Link electrons to chlorine volume**
Write the anode half equation:
$$2\text{Cl}^- \rightarrow \text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{e}^-$$
Two moles of electrons make one mole of $\text{Cl}_2$, so:
$$n(\text{Cl}_2) = \frac{0.252}{2} = 0.126 \text{ mol}$$
At room conditions one mole of gas occupies $24 \text{ dm}^3$:
$$V = 0.126 \times 24 = 3.02 \text{ dm}^3$$

Link electrons to sodium mass**
Write the cathode half equation:
$$\text{Na}^+ + \text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Na}$$
One mole of electrons makes one mole of $\text{Na}$, so $n(\text{Na}) = 0.252 \text{ mol}$:
$$m = n \times M = 0.252 \times 23.0 = 5.79 \text{ g}$$

Final answer: volume of chlorine = $3.02 \text{ dm}^3$
mass of sodium = $5.79 \text{ g}$

hints: Recall that any $E^\ominus$ is measured against the standard hydrogen electrode, so you need two half-cells joined by a salt bridge and a voltmeter.
Think about why this manganese half-cell needs an inert $\text{Pt}$ electrode and must contain both $\text{MnO}_4^-$ and $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ plus $\text{H}^+$ in the same beaker.
List the standard conditions that must be labelled: concentration $1.0 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ for ions, $298 \text{ K}$, and $1 \text{ atm}$ for $\text{H}_2$.
Remember the hydrogen half-cell needs a $\text{Pt}$ electrode with $\text{H}_2$ gas bubbled over it into $1.0 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{H}^+$ solution.
walkthrough:
Picture the two half-cells side by side**
Imagine two beakers. One is your unknown manganese half-cell, the other is the standard hydrogen electrode reference. Join the solutions with a salt bridge dipping into both, and join the electrodes with a wire through a high resistance voltmeter.

Build the manganese side correctly**
Because both $\text{MnO}_4^-$ and $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ are in solution, there is no metal rod to use. Dip an inert $\text{Pt}$ (or graphite) electrode into a single beaker containing $\text{MnO}_4^-$, $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ and $\text{H}^+$. Label one solute as $1.0 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$, typically $\text{MnO}_4^-$ and $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ both at $1.0 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ and $\text{H}^+$ at $1.0 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$.

Build the hydrogen side correctly**
In the second beaker place $1.0 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{H}^+$ solution with a $\text{Pt}$ electrode. Bubble $\text{H}_2(\text{g})$ at $1 \text{ atm}$ over the electrode using a gas inlet tube. Label $\text{H}_2(\text{g})$, the delivery system, and the $\text{Pt}$ electrode.

Add the essential labels for standard conditions**
Clearly label the salt bridge touching both solutions, the voltmeter in the external circuit, and temperature $298 \text{ K}$. Without $1.0 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ concentrations, $298 \text{ K}$ and $1 \text{ atm}$ $\text{H}_2$, the measured voltage is not a standard potential.

Final answer: Left beaker: $\text{MnO}_4^-$, $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ and $\text{H}^+$ (all $1.0 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$) with $\text{Pt}$ electrode. Right beaker: $\text{H}^+$ ($1.0 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$) with $\text{Pt}$ electrode and $\text{H}_2$ gas at $1 \text{ atm}$ bubbled over it. Beakers joined by salt bridge, electrodes joined by voltmeter, temperature $298 \text{ K}$ labelled.

hints: Look in the Data Booklet for a half-cell with $E^\ominus$ more positive than $+1.52 \text{ V}$, because only a stronger oxidising agent can oxidise $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ to $\text{MnO}_4^-$.
Combine the reduction half equation of your chosen oxidant with the reverse of the $\text{MnO}_4^-$ / $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ equation, balancing electrons, $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
walkthrough:
Choose a stronger oxidising agent**
$E^\ominus = +1.52 \text{ V}$ tells you $\text{MnO}_4^-$ is a very strong oxidant. To force the reverse, oxidising $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ up to $\text{MnO}_4^-$, you need an even stronger oxidant with a more positive $E^\ominus$. From the Data Booklet, $\text{F}_2$ with $E^\ominus = +2.87 \text{ V}$ works well:
$$\text{F}_2 + 2\text{e}^- \rightleftharpoons 2\text{F}^-$$

Combine the half equations**
Reverse the manganese reduction to an oxidation and multiply to cancel $10\text{e}^-$:
$$2\text{Mn}^{2+} + 8\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{MnO}_4^- + 16\text{H}^+ + 10\text{e}^-$$
$$5\text{F}_2 + 10\text{e}^- \rightarrow 10\text{F}^-$$
Adding gives the overall balanced equation:
$$2\text{Mn}^{2+} + 8\text{H}_2\text{O} + 5\text{F}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MnO}_4^- + 16\text{H}^+ + 10\text{F}^-$$
